newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU says complex patent system costly for companies.
newsitem.headline: EU says complex patent system costly for companies.

text.p: The European Commission, concerned that Europe is lagging behind its main competitors in new high-tech industries, said on Wednesday the system of patents in the 15-nation bloc was both complex and costly.
The European Union executive adopted a discussion paper to launch wide-ranging consultations on how to reform the system, in which European and national patents exist side by side.
A single EU-wide patent would have several advantages in protecting innovations, including better legal certainty and the need for only one patent application, it said.
"The present system of patents in the Union is complex and expensive, and does not provide a unitary patent for all member states," said EU Internal Market Commission Mario Monti.
"We have to see to it that innovations can enjoy the same protection throughout the single market in order to develop the role played by innovation in competitiveness and job creation."

Companies doing business in the EU still did not have access to a single system of patent protection because the 1975 Luxembourg Convention, which was to establish such a system, had never come into force as it had only been ratified by seven member states.
"The Community must seek to remove the political and practical obstacles that remain, preventing the single market from realising its full potential," the Commission said.
It asked whether the intergovernmental convention should be replaced by EU legislation ensuring that firms could secure patent protection throughout the bloc with a single application.

"A unitary Community patent would have the advantage that its effects would be the same throughout the Union; it could be granted, transferred, revoked or allowed to lapse only in respect of the whole of the Union."
"Applicants would need to make one application only, the management of patent rights would be simplified, duplication of legal actions would be avoided, and legal certainty would be improved."

The EU executive noted that Europe had an "excellent scientific base" but was less successful in converting its skills into new products and market share, especially in sectors such as information and communication technology.
The EU was also trailing behind both the United States and Japan in research.

Improving the patent system in Europe would not in itself reverse this trend, it stressed. This could only be achieved by a fundamental reorganisation of European research. But the patent system must not act as a further brake on the competitiveness of European companies.
"Ease of obtaining patents, legal certainty, appropriate geographic coverage: these are all essential criteria for the effective protection of innovation in the European Union."

UNICE, the European employers' organisation, agreed that it cost too much to obtain patents in Europe. "It is definitely too expensive, especially if you compare it with the cost of patents in the United States and Japan," said Jerome Chauven, adviser at UNICE's company affairs department.

He said UNICE would in principle be in favour of an EU patent, but cautioned that it would be too expensive if it had to be translated into all the Union's languages. In addition, UNICE wanted to retain national patents, leaving it to individual firms to choose which one to use.

The Commission said its consultations with industry, inventors, as well as with member states, would culminate with a hearing in November. "The Commission will then be in a position to determine its legislative agenda."
